items.title: Jensen Huang goes on CNBC Squawk Box: AMD's 10% warrant to OpenAI is 'surprising' and 'imaginative' — 'they're giving away 10% of the company before they even built it' — Nvidia stock gains on the comment as Huang reframes the deal rather than dismissing it, and Nvidia's own ~$100B OpenAI commitment comes back into focus
items.summary: **Afternoon follow-up to Monday's T1**: on CNBC's Squawk Box Wednesday morning, **Jensen Huang gave Nvidia's first on-camera reaction** to the Monday AMD-OpenAI 6 GW / 10%-warrant deal. The specific quote: AMD's offer is **'surprising'** and **'imaginative'**, and 'I'm surprised that they would give away 10% of the company before they even built it. And so anyhow, it's clever, I guess.' The tone read as **mildly sarcastic but strategically generous** — Huang chose to characterize the deal structure (not AMD's chips) as the newsworthy move, which is a specifically different posture from either dismissing AMD on technical grounds or escalating the rivalry. **Market reaction**: Nvidia stock gained on the comments, extending Tuesday's ~1% recovery to ~$186.80 after Monday's 1.5% dip (now covered in today's am item). The read on the Street is that Huang's commentary **implicitly endorses the 'additive, not displaced' framing** that Melius Research used Tuesday morning when raising Nvidia's price target to $275 from $240. **The second-order question Huang's framing surfaces**: Nvidia's own ~$100B OpenAI investment pledge from September 2025 has been **repeatedly walked back** — Huang said in February 2026 the $100B figure was 'never a commitment,' and in March 2026 at a Morgan Stanley conference called the full $100B 'probably not in the cards' because of OpenAI's planned IPO. **If Huang's Wednesday CNBC frame is 'AMD overpaid in equity to lock OpenAI in'**, the implicit comparison is to Nvidia's own structure, which has stayed deliberately flexible (nonbinding MoU, up to $100B, 'one round at a time'). **What this changes vs. the am item**: the am framed the deal via analyst reaction (Jefferies $300 target, Melius $275 Nvidia target); the pm now has **Nvidia's own CEO on record characterizing the warrant structure as unusual enough to be worth naming on live TV** — which is specifically the signal analysts are now using to argue that the AMD warrant pattern may NOT be copied by Oracle or CoreWeave on their next renegotiations, because Nvidia's reaction establishes that at least one supplier views equity-aligned-to-execution as a structural overcommitment rather than a template.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is the specific 'the biggest Monday AI story got Nvidia's CEO on CNBC making a live-TV comment about it 48 hours later, and his word choice is the actual newsworthy part' item — a straight extension of this morning's am T1. Three concrete things worth filing. First, the specific **'imaginative'-and-'surprising' word choice from Huang** is the specific concrete signal that **Nvidia's playbook is to frame the AMD deal as a structural curiosity, not a competitive threat** — a specifically different stance from (a) technical dismissal ('MI450 won't match our GPUs on throughput') or (b) counter-escalation ('we'll match the warrant terms'). For a Python hobbyist, the practical read: **when the dominant supplier chooses to downplay a specific move by a smaller competitor on live TV, that is the specific signal that the smaller competitor's move is actually working** — if Huang thought AMD's deal was commercially irrelevant he'd have ignored it, and if he thought it was existentially threatening he'd have counter-escalated; the specific middle choice ('clever, I guess') is what you say when a competitor just locked in your biggest customer's second-source commitment and you are deliberately not giving them more oxygen. Second, the specific **callback to Nvidia's own ~$100B OpenAI commitment** is the specific concrete context that makes Huang's comment land differently than it first reads. For a Python hobbyist, the practical read: **Nvidia has quietly been walking back the $100B figure for most of 2026** — February 'never a commitment,' March 'probably not in the cards' due to OpenAI's IPO — so Huang characterizing AMD's warrant as 'giving away 10% before you built it' is specifically a frame that **retroactively legitimizes Nvidia's own nonbinding-MoU structure** as the responsible choice. The specific signal to watch: **whether Nvidia's walk-back of the $100B figure continues or reverses in the weeks ahead** — if the Nvidia commitment firms up with specific numbers in response to AMD, that's the real competitive counter-move; the CNBC words are just the setup. Third, the specific **implication for Oracle and CoreWeave's next contract renegotiations** is the specific concrete read on what this means for the broader compute buildout. For a Python hobbyist, the practical read: **the AM item's framing was that the AMD warrant structure might become a template** (equity-aligned-to-execution replacing take-or-pay); Huang's Wednesday CNBC framing **cuts against that read** by establishing on the record that at least one major supplier characterizes the structure as a specific overcommitment rather than a sensible pattern. If Oracle and CoreWeave now **DON'T** renegotiate their contracts with warrant structures over the next quarter, Huang's CNBC commentary is the specific moment that framing died. Practical concrete next step: watch Nvidia's **Q3 FY2027 earnings commentary later this fall** (the specific company reporting cycle that will next give Nvidia a chance to address the AMD deal publicly) for whether the ~$100B figure comes back with firmer numbers, or whether the AMD-OpenAI deal is treated as 'additive to a growing market' and left there — the specific earnings call language will tell you more about where the compute market is actually headed than any analyst note between now and then.

items.title: OpenAI's November 12, 2026 cutoff for serving its models through SpaceX-owned Cursor is now five weeks out — Cursor CEO Michael Truell says OpenAI models account for ~5% of Cursor traffic (Composer, Claude, Grok and Gemini make up the rest); developers can keep using OpenAI models by supplying their own API keys, Astra specifically excluded even during wind-down
items.summary: **Five-week countdown**: November 12, 2026 is the proposed end date for OpenAI serving its models (GPT-6 Sol, Luna, and the coming Astra family) through Cursor's integrated model picker, following SpaceX's August 14 completion of its $60B acquisition of Cursor's parent company Anysphere. **The reason OpenAI gave in its August 29 letter**: a change-of-control provision in its agreement with Cursor was triggered by the SpaceX acquisition, and OpenAI 'cannot be confident SpaceX will use its technology within the terms of service' based on 'our experience with Elon Musk's companies violating contracts' — a specific callback to Twitter's post-acquisition contract violations and xAI's admitted TOS breach. **What is NOT cut off**: Developers can continue using OpenAI models inside Cursor **by supplying their own OpenAI API keys** — the shutoff is for Cursor's integrated model-router (where OpenAI models are billed through Cursor's subscription), not for direct OpenAI API usage. **What IS cut off even during the wind-down**: OpenAI's upcoming **Astra** family (and any future models) will not be served through Cursor at all, meaning Cursor Pro's integrated model picker will not include OpenAI's post-GPT-6 generation. **Scale and impact per Cursor CEO Michael Truell**: OpenAI models account for **~5% of Cursor's user traffic** — the heavy majority of Cursor runs on Anthropic's Claude family, Cursor's own in-house **Composer** model, Google's Gemini, and (post-SpaceX) xAI's **Grok**. The specific migration path Cursor is leaning on is **Grok as the primary SpaceXAI-aligned alternative** — same corporate family, no change-of-control risk. **The 'OpenAI is leaving Cursor in November' framing from Tom's Guide earlier in September has aged into a specific calendar milestone that developers now need to plan around**. For hobbyists on Cursor Pro: the practical read is that the integrated OpenAI models will stop working on Nov 12 unless you add a personal OpenAI API key to your Cursor settings, which Cursor's docs explicitly support. **The wider ecosystem read**: this is the first time a major LLM provider has publicly cited **ownership-based distrust** as the reason for cutting off a developer-tooling partner — and it establishes a specific precedent that **model-provider contracts have change-of-control clauses that get enforced when they trigger**, which will show up in future SaaS M&A due diligence for any company whose product depends on third-party LLM API access.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: this is the specific 'if you use Cursor, here is the specific calendar date you have to plan around, and here is the exact workaround that keeps your workflow unchanged' item — pure practical developer-tooling news. Three concrete things worth filing. First, the specific **November 12 cutoff date** is the specific concrete event-horizon. For a Python hobbyist on Cursor Pro, the practical read: **you have about five weeks to decide between (a) migrating off OpenAI models in your Cursor usage** (easy — Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 are already the heavy-majority default inside Cursor, as are Cursor's own Composer and Google's Gemini), **or (b) adding your personal OpenAI API key to Cursor's settings** to keep using GPT-6 Sol/Luna through your own paid API account. **Option (b) is slightly more work and loses the convenience of unified billing, but keeps your current model mix intact.** The specific unlock here is **Cursor explicitly supports BYO-key**: this isn't a loophole, it's documented. Second, the specific **~5% of Cursor traffic uses OpenAI models figure** from Michael Truell is the specific concrete signal that **the OpenAI cutoff is a smaller operational hit than the headline suggests** — the Claude family (and increasingly Composer) are already doing the heavy lifting on Cursor. For a Python hobbyist, the practical read: **if you've been defaulting to Claude Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 for coding inside Cursor** (as most users have — see the Vals Index numbers in prior digests), you will not notice the OpenAI cutoff happen. **The one specific case where you'll feel it: if you've been using Codex/GPT-6 for a specific style of code the Claude family handles differently** (anything where you deliberately want OpenAI's specific tool-use quirks or reasoning style), you'll need the BYO-key path. The specific implication of 'Astra specifically excluded during wind-down': **OpenAI is not just drawing down the current contract, it's deliberately keeping its upcoming next-gen model out of Cursor entirely** — so the long-term read is 'OpenAI's next-gen capabilities will be inside Codex and ChatGPT, not Cursor', and if you want to try Astra when it ships you'll do so through OpenAI's own tools, not through Cursor. Third, the specific **'change-of-control provision cited and enforced' precedent** is the specific concrete signal to file for how AI developer tooling contracts work going forward. For a Python hobbyist, the practical read: **every AI-tooling company that depends on third-party LLM API access now has a specific M&A risk that was previously treated as hypothetical**. The specific implication: when you choose a developer tool that bundles LLM access (Cursor, Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Zed, Aider), **you're also implicitly choosing a specific corporate relationship between that tool and the LLM providers**, and that relationship can be severed by an acquisition that triggers change-of-control. The specific hedging strategy: **prefer BYO-key setups over bundled subscriptions when the long-term relationship between the tool and the model matters to you** — the extra friction of managing your own API keys is the price of insulation from future ownership-based cutoffs. Practical concrete next step: **if you use Cursor, log into your settings now (not Nov 11) and verify you have a personal OpenAI API key configured as a fallback** — the specific moment to not want to be setting that up is when the cutoff actually hits and the integrated models suddenly stop responding mid-session. If you don't use OpenAI models in Cursor at all, you can ignore this and nothing changes.
items.why_it_matters_brief: The November 12 cutoff for OpenAI models in SpaceX-owned Cursor is now five weeks out — only ~5% of Cursor traffic uses OpenAI models (Claude, Composer, Gemini and Grok carry the rest), and BYO API keys will keep GPT-6 working inside Cursor; the real signal is the first public ownership-based LLM cutoff and its precedent for AI-tooling M&A.
